nameStory: Queen of the prairie earned her royal title from her commanding presence in wild meadows and prairies across the Midwest and Northeast. Standing tall above other wildflowers with her delicate pink crown of blooms, she truly rules over her grassy domain like botanical royalty.
description: Queen of the prairie is a stately perennial wildflower that can tower 4-6 feet tall when happy. It produces large, airy clusters of tiny pink flowers that look like cotton candy clouds floating above deeply divided, fern-like leaves. This member of the rose family prefers moist soils and creates impressive colonies over time, making it a showstopper in naturalized gardens and wet meadows.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Fluffy, cloud-like clusters of tiny pink flowers with a sweet, honey-like fragrance that attracts butterflies from far away

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, fern-like leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, with sharply pointed leaflets

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and sturdy stems that stand firm even in wind, growing 4-6 feet high with flowers held well above the foliage

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, twisted seed capsules that spiral like tiny corkscrews and persist into fall

habitat: Queen of the prairie thrives in moist meadows, wet prairies, and the edges of marshes throughout New England, though it's more common in cultivation than in the wild here. Look for it in full sun to partial shade areas with consistently moist soil, often near streams or in low-lying areas that stay damp. It's frequently planted in rain gardens and naturalized landscapes.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as reddish shoots that unfurl into the characteristic ferny foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season arrives in mid to late summer with spectacular pink flower clusters that last for several weeks.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads while leaves may turn golden yellow before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, with only the twisted seed heads sometimes persisting above snow.

funFact: Despite being called 'queen of the prairie,' this plant is actually more closely related to roses than to prairie grasses, and its tiny flowers contain the same compounds that give roses their sweet fragrance!
confusionNotes: Queen of the prairie is most often confused with meadowsweet, but queen of the prairie has pink flowers while meadowsweet has white or cream-colored blooms. Remember: 'Pink for the Prairie Queen' to keep them straight.
contextualKnowledge: Though native to North American prairies, queen of the prairie is more commonly seen in New England gardens than in wild habitats, as our region sits at the eastern edge of its natural range where suitable prairie habitat is limited.
compareHints: Queen of the prairie stands out from its meadowsweet cousins by its pink flowers and taller stature - meadowsweet has white or cream flowers and typically grows shorter. Giant meadowsweet can match its height but has white flowers, while dropwort is much smaller with white flowers and prefers drier soils.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Meadowsweet is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, though you might occasionally encounter queen of the prairie which has pink flowers instead of white.
Dropwort is much smaller and more delicate than its cousin meadowsweet, with finer, more divided leaves and smaller flower clusters.
Giant meadowsweet dwarfs its relatives - regular meadowsweet typically grows 3-4 feet tall with smaller flower clusters, while queen of the prairie has pink flowers instead of white.
